quote: 8.1 By Commerce One. Commerce One shall indemnify, defend and hold harmless Corio and its Customers from any and all damages, liabilities, costs and expenses (including reasonable attorneys' fees) incurred by Corio or its Customers arising out of any claim that the Software infringes any patent, copyright, trademark or trade right secret of a third party; provided that Corio or its Customer promptly notifies Commerce One in writing of any such claim and promptly tenders the control and the defense and settlement of any such claim to Commerce One
rationale: Section 8.1 gives us (and our Customers) a Vendor-side third-party IP indemnity with an express duty to defend, covering patent, copyright, trademark and trade secret claims relating to the Software, with the usual notice/control/cooperation mechanics. The exclusions in Section 8.2 are the customary ones (use outside the Documentation; modification by a party other than Commerce One), and Section 8.1 carries the full remedy ladder — procure the right to continue use, replace or modify to make the Software non-infringing, and failing that terminate and refund a pro-rated portion of fees paid. On the cap, Section 9 expressly carves Section 8 liability out of both the 12-month payment cap and the consequential-damages exclusion, so the indemnity is uncapped — better for us than the fallback's 3x annual fees super-cap. No Corio-side indemnity exists anywhere in the Agreement, so there is no one-way exposure to narrow. This clause therefore sits at (and in places above) the fallback position and is not redlined. Short of preferred only in minor respects that we note rather than flag: the indemnified subject matter is the "Software" rather than also the MarketSite.net Service, and there is no separate cover for Commerce One's breach of law, Commerce One-caused data breach, or gross negligence/wilful misconduct.

Intent is preserved: the retained sentence about negotiating ownership of Software enhancements still functions (the new proviso only bars joint ownership as an outcome), the assignment sentence still reads coherently after the deletion, and no cross-reference or defined term is orphaned. Drafting nits to tidy (not defects in element coverage): the new data sentence is rendered without a section number — give it a number (e.g. 13.6) and anchor it in Section 13 rather than after the successors fragment; and consider using the defined "Corio Services" instead of lower-case "services under this Agreement" so the processing limitation tracks a defined scope. quote: 11.2 Termination. If either party materially breaches any term or condition of this Agreement and fails to cure such breach within-thirty (30) days after receiving written notice of the breach, the nonbreaching party may terminate this Agreement on written notice at any time following the end of such-thirty (30) day period.

That fails both preferred and fallback in a multi-year term, so we target the preferred level with one new Section 11.3, numbered inline to match the Section 11 scheme: Corio (our client, the customer under this Agreement) may terminate for convenience on 30 days' prior written notice, Commerce One refunds prepaid fees pro rata for the post-termination period, and Commerce One has no convenience termination right during the initial or any renewal term. The right is stated in Corio's name rather than as "the customer" because "CUSTOMER(S)" is a defined term meaning Corio's sublicensees (§ 1.6), so generic customer wording would create a definitional conflict. The § 11.1 mutual non-renewal notice is natural-term non-renewal (a RENEWAL matter effective at expiration) and is left verbatim, not flagged as a Vendor mid-term convenience right.

ops.newText: Neither party may assign this Agreement or any rights or obligations hereunder, whether by operation of law or otherwise, without the prior written consent of the other party, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld.
ops.oldText: Neither party may assign this Agreement or any rights or obligations hereunder, whether by operation of law or otherwise, without the prior written consent of the other party.

proposal.summary: Add a reasonableness standard to assignment consent and a written-notice requirement for successor assignments in Section 14.1.

quote: 14.1 Assignment. Neither party may assign this Agreement or any rights or obligations hereunder, whether by operation of law or otherwise, without the prior written consent of the other party. Notwithstanding the foregoing, either party shall have the right to assign this Agreement in connection with the merger or acquisition of such party or the sale of all or substantially all of its assets related to this Agreement without such consent, except in the case where such transaction involves a direct competitor of the other party where consent of the other party will be required.
rationale: Section 14.1 is mutual and already carries a successor carve-out (merger, acquisition or sale of substantially all assets without consent) and a consent requirement for other assignments, and there is no change-of-control termination or re-pricing right anywhere (Sections 11.1-11.2 contain only non-renewal, breach and insolvency triggers), so this is not walk-away territory. It nevertheless fails the fallback on two material terms: consent is at each party's absolute discretion with no "not unreasonably withheld" standard (which matters most where Commerce One asserts an acquirer is a "direct competitor"), and there is no written-notice mechanic for successor assignments. We target the fallback rather than the asymmetric preferred position because rewriting this mutual clause into a Vendor-only restriction would require collateral changes; the missing affiliate carve-out and competitor limb are noted but not pressed at this level.

elements.element: Customer may assign to an affiliate without consent.
elements.evidence: Section 14.1 as rendered contains only a merger/acquisition/sale-of-assets carve-out; there is no affiliate carve-out anywhere in the clause, so an affiliate transfer still needs Vendor's prior written consent.

elements.element: Customer may assign to a successor in a merger, acquisition, or sale of substantially all assets without consent.
elements.evidence: The carve-out is qualified: 'except in the case where such transaction involves a direct competitor of the other party where consent of the other party will be required.' Customer's successor assignment is therefore not consent-free in every M&A scenario.

elements.element: Vendor may not assign without Customer's consent.
elements.evidence: The retained second sentence lets 'either party' — including Vendor — assign on its own merger, acquisition or asset sale 'without such consent', so Vendor can assign without Customer's consent.

elements.element: Customer's consent to Vendor assignment is not to be unreasonably withheld.
elements.evidence: Inserted: 'without the prior written consent of the other party, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld.'

elements.element: Vendor may never assign to a Customer competitor.
elements.evidence: The competitor limb is a consent trigger, not a prohibition: 'where such transaction involves a direct competitor of the other party where consent of the other party will be required.' A Vendor assignment to a Customer competitor remains possible with consent.

elements.element: Customer's change of control gives Vendor no termination right.
elements.evidence: No change-of-control termination or re-pricing right appears in Section 14.1 or in the termination provisions identified (Sections 11.1-11.2 carry only non-renewal, breach and insolvency triggers); the condition therefore does not arise.

elements.element: Both parties may assign to a successor.
elements.evidence: Retained: 'either party shall have the right to assign this Agreement in connection with the merger or acquisition of such party or the sale of all or substantially all of its assets related to this Agreement'; the competitor limb only shifts such a transfer back into the consent regime, it does not bar successor assignment.

elements.element: A successor assignment requires written notice.
elements.evidence: Inserted proviso in the successor sentence: 'provided the assigning party gives the other party written notice.'

elements.element: Other assignments require consent.
elements.evidence: Retained first sentence: 'Neither party may assign this Agreement or any rights or obligations hereunder, whether by operation of law or otherwise, without the prior written consent of the other party.' The only no-consent exception retained is the successor carve-out; no affiliate or other non-successor exception exists.

elements.element: Consent to other assignments is not to be unreasonably withheld.
elements.evidence: The inserted standard attaches directly to the general consent requirement governing all non-successor assignments: 'which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld.'

verification.notes: Fallback level is complete: the two inserted edits supply the only missing elements (reasonableness standard and successor written-notice), and the existing mutual successor carve-out plus consent requirement already supply the other two. Preferred level is not reached: no affiliate carve-out for Customer, the successor right is still cut back by the direct-competitor consent proviso, Vendor retains a consent-free successor assignment right, and the competitor limb is a consent trigger rather than an absolute bar on assignment to a Customer competitor. To reach preferred, the drafter would need to add 'Customer may assign to an affiliate without Vendor's consent', remove the competitor proviso as applied to Customer, restrict the successor carve-out to Customer only, and add an express prohibition on Vendor assigning to a Customer competitor. Minimal: only two insertions, no deletions, no survival tails, procedures or extra requirements outside the fallback checklist; favourable retained language (mutual successor carve-out, competitor protection, null-and-void enforcement) is preserved. Preserves intent: the consent regime, competitor protection, successors-and-assigns and null-and-void mechanics all survive without contradiction; no undefined terms or dangling cross-references are created. 'Deviation' is the correct pre-redline classification because the original clause failed two material fallback terms (no reasonableness standard on consent; no written-notice mechanic for successor assignments), while remaining outside walk-away territory given the M&A carve-out and the absence of any change-of-control termination or re-pricing right.

quote: This Agreement shall be governed by the laws of the State of California, USA, excluding conflict of laws provisions and excluding the 1980 United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods. Any disputes arising out of this Agreement shall be resolved by binding arbitration in accordance with the then-current commercial arbitration rules of the American Arbitration Association
rationale: California governing law is acceptable at the fallback level and is already met. However, Section 14.3 sends all disputes to mandatory binding AAA arbitration before a single arbitrator rather than to the corresponding California courts, so the forum element of the fallback fails on a material term (the reference to courts is only for entering judgment on the award). The arbitration seat is domestic, so this is a deviation rather than walk-away. We target the fallback: retain California law and substitute exclusive jurisdiction of the state and federal courts in San Francisco County, deleting the now-redundant arbitration machinery and conforming the Section 12.2 cross-reference to arbitration so no dangling mechanic remains. We did not add the temporary-injunctive-relief carve-out, which belongs to the preferred position only.

verification.notes: The fallback checklist is complete: California law is retained (already met) and the arbitration forum is replaced with exclusive jurisdiction of the California state and federal courts in San Francisco County, which is the forum corresponding to the retained governing law. The preferred level is not reached because neither New York law nor New York County courts are proposed; that is acknowledged and acceptable because the redline targets the fallback. Minimality holds. Only the jurisdiction/forum words were changed: the conflict-of-laws exclusion, the CISG exclusion and the balance of Section 14.3 survive verbatim. The deleted sentences (AAA rules reference, single-arbitrator appointment, judgment-on-award, AAA fee allocation) are all arbitration-specific machinery that could not survive removal of arbitration without contradiction, so their deletion is necessary rather than cosmetic. No extras (no injunctive-relief carve-out, no fee-shifting substitute, no procedure or survival tail) were added. Intent is preserved. The heading is conformed to "Choice of Law; Venue," and the Section 12.2 cross-reference is changed from "referred to arbitration in the manner provided in Section 14.3" to "resolved in the manner provided in Section 14.3," so the escalation mechanic (ten business days of officer negotiation, then referral) still functions and no dangling reference to arbitration remains. The termination triggers, cure period and notice mechanics in that paragraph are untouched. Residual point for the drafter to confirm, not a defect on the record shown: the defined term "RULES" was created in the deleted arbitration sentence. It is used only within the deleted text here, but confirm no other section of the Agreement references "Rules," which would otherwise leave an undefined term. Classification as a deviation is correct: the seat was domestic (San Francisco), so the original clause was not walk-away, but mandatory binding arbitration defeats the fallback forum element on a material term and warranted a redline.

verification.notes: Fallback level is complete: the single inserted affiliate-extension clause supplies the notice-conditioned affiliate coverage, and the retained Section 14.1 M&A assignment right (incorporated into the Section 2 grants by the "except in accordance with Section 14.1" proviso) supplies successor transferability. Preferred remains incomplete on two elements: (a) no contractor extension anywhere in Section 2, and (b) the fully paid-up Section 2.2 grant is perpetual but not expressly irrevocable. These are the exact operative repairs needed if the preferred level is pursued. Minimality holds: one concise insertion addressing only the failing fallback element, with a short parenthetical control definition necessary because "affiliate" is otherwise undefined in the Agreement. Corio is a single defined entity, so there is no duplicate affiliate coverage; Sections 2.1, 2.2, 2.10 and 14.1 are left verbatim, with no survival tails, expense language, or other extras. quote: 4.1 License Fees. In consideration for the licenses granted to Corio pursuant to Section 2 of this Agreement, Corio shall pay the license fees specified in EXHIBIT B hereto. Payment terms of such license fees shall be as set forth in EXHIBIT B hereto.
rationale: No most-favoured-nation or price/terms-matching obligation runs against Corio (our party) anywhere in the Agreement. Fees are fixed by reference to Exhibit B (Sections 4.1-4.2; Exhibit B Pricing and Revenue Sharing Fees at p0152-p0161), with no obligation for Corio to extend Commerce One terms no less favourable than those given to any third party, and no right-to-match or best-offer mechanic. Searches for most-favoured/favourable-terms, matching, comparable-customer, lowest-price and discount language returned nothing, and the Grant of Rights (Section 2), Shared Resources (Section 13), Payment Terms and the Exhibit D sales and marketing cooperation provisions (expressly non-binding) contain no such covenant. The Agreement therefore meets our preferred position (no Customer MFN); no redline proposed.

quote: Corio to pay Commerce One [*] of all Application Management Revenue from Corio Customers for use of Commerce One Software or MarketSite.net Service Access subject to the following limitations.
rationale: The Agreement imposes no minimum purchase or volume commitment on Corio and meets the preferred position. Exhibit B prices Software Users as "Unlimited" (p0151), the licence fee is a one-time amount due on Software Acceptance (p0152, p0165), and the MarketSite.net access and maintenance fees are annual fees for services actually made available (p0153, p0154, p0168), with maintenance continuing only "provided that Corio continues to pay" (p0055) rather than being a guaranteed spend. Variable fees track actual activity: Application Management Revenue share is a percentage of revenue actually invoiced to Corio Customers (p0157) and implementation work is on a time-and-materials basis capped at a stated maximum (p0161); further professional services and training arise only at Corio's request and by mutual agreement (p0068, p0067). There is no committed user count, no minimum guarantee, no take-or-pay and no shortfall penalty. Two points noted but not flagged: the 40-Authorized-Software-User "minimum limitation" in p0158 is a qualifying condition for the royalty-free use of the initial 3000 licences, not a purchase obligation or usage cap; and the "shortfall" reference in the audit clause (p0059) is a reciprocal true-up of under/overpayments, which is expressly the treatment our playbook prefers. Accordingly no redline is proposed.

The pricing exhibit fixes fees for "Year 2-5, and beyond" and neither Section 4 nor Exhibit B/Payment Terms grants Commerce One any renewal uplift right, so the price-increase elements at both levels are inapplicable. ops.text: Transition Assistance and Data Return. Upon expiration or termination of this Agreement for any reason, Commerce One shall (a) at Corio's request, provide reasonable transition assistance to Corio for a period of at least ninety (90) days following such expiration or termination; and (b) within thirty (30) days after such expiration or termination, export and deliver to Corio all data belonging to, supplied by or processed for Corio or its Customers that is in Commerce One's possession or control.

elements.evidence: Rendered 7.3: Software (defined term) "will perform in substantial accordance with the Documentation ... for a period of ninety (90) days from the Effective Date (the "Warranty Period")"; the December 31, 1999 outside cap that would have truncated the 90 days (Effective Date 29 Oct 1999) is deleted.

verification.notes: Fallback checklist is complete: 90-day software-to-Documentation warranty, the same 90-day cover for the MarketSite.net Service (>30 days), and the retained correction/replacement and prepaid-fee refund remedies. Deviation status is correct at the original: the 60-day period, further capped at December 31, 1999, fell below the 90-day software fallback minimum, and the disclaimer reaches only implied warranties so the express warranty survives. Both edits are necessary: 60 -> 90 days to reach the threshold, and deletion of the "but in no event not later than December 31, 1999" outside date, which (from a 29 October 1999 Effective Date) would otherwise truncate the new 90-day period to roughly 63 days. No surplus language, procedures, survival tails or extra warranties were added, so minimality holds. Intent preserved: the defined term "Warranty Period" is retained in place, so cross-references in Sections 7.3, 7.4 and 11.2 remain intact; remedies, the exclusive-remedy sentence, the media warranty and the exclusions list are untouched. Preferred level remains incomplete for the professional-and-workmanlike standard, the 12-month software period and the compliance-with-laws warranty; these are correctly flagged as noted-not-pursued rather than inserted. Minor point for the drafter's awareness only (not a defect against the checklist): the 90 days runs from the Effective Date rather than from delivery/acceptance, so practical cover may be shorter than a delivery-anchored period if deployment is delayed.

mappings.element: Vendor may audit no more than once per year.
mappings.quote: Such inspections may be made no more than once each calendar year

mappings.element: Vendor must give at least 15 days' notice of an audit.
Vendor bears audit costs unless underpayment exceeds 10 percent.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] We can accept an annual records inspection, but we need a fixed notice period rather than "reasonable notice", so we have set at least fifteen (15) days. We have also aligned the cost-shifting trigger with our position that Commerce One bears the cost of the inspection unless it reveals an underpayment of more than ten percent (10%).

ops.newText: Such inspections may be made no more than once each calendar year, at reasonable times and upon at least fifteen (15) days' notice.
ops.oldText: Such inspections may be made no more than once each calendar year, at reasonable times and upon reasonable notice.

proposal.summary: Fix audit notice period and underpayment cost-shifting threshold in Section 4.4

quote: Such inspections may be made no more than once each calendar year, at reasonable times and upon reasonable notice. Commerce One shall bear all costs and expenses of such inspection.
rationale: Section 4.4 is the only audit/inspection right binding Corio (books and records supporting amounts payable to Commerce One); no other verification or systems-access right exists in the Agreement or Exhibits. The clause already limits inspections to once each calendar year, uses an independent certified public accountant reasonably acceptable to Corio, and places costs on Commerce One, and it gives no direct access to Corio systems. It fails the fallback on two material terms: notice is only "reasonable notice" rather than a fixed minimum period, and the cost-shifting trigger is an underpayment of more than 5% rather than the 10% fallback threshold. We therefore fixed notice at fifteen (15) days and moved the reimbursement trigger to more than ten percent (10%), leaving the rest of the clause untouched. Preferred-level extras (30 days' notice, express business-hours and confidentiality wording, off-site where possible) are noted but not pursued given the clause otherwise sits at or above the fallback.

elements.element: Vendor may audit no more than once in any 12-month period.
elements.evidence: Rendered clause says "Such inspections may be made no more than once each calendar year". A calendar-year cap permits inspections in December and the following January, so it is not literally a limit of once in any rolling 12-month period. To meet the preferred element the drafter would need "no more than once in any twelve (12) month period".

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 30 days' written notice of an audit.
elements.evidence: Rendered clause requires "at least fifteen (15) days' notice" — short of 30 days, and the notice is not expressed as written notice.

elements.element: Audits occur during business hours.
elements.evidence: Clause says only "at reasonable times"; no business-hours limitation was inserted.

elements.element: Audits are conducted by an independent auditor.
elements.evidence: "open for inspection by an independent certified public accountant reasonably acceptable to Corio" — retained existing language satisfies independence.

elements.element: The auditor is bound by confidentiality obligations.
elements.evidence: Section 4.4 contains no confidentiality undertaking from or on behalf of the inspecting accountant, and none was added.

elements.element: Audits are conducted off-site where possible.
elements.evidence: No off-site preference appears in the rendered clause; inspection location is unaddressed.

elements.element: Vendor bears audit costs unless underpayment exceeds 5 percent.
elements.evidence: As rendered, cost shifts only on "an underpayment of more than ten percent (10%)", not 5 percent. (Note the 10% trigger is more Customer-favourable than the preferred 5% figure and is required by the fallback element, but it does not literally satisfy the preferred wording.)

elements.element: Vendor has no direct access to Customer systems for an audit.
elements.evidence: The right extends only to "books of accounts and records for determining the amounts payable"; no systems, network or remote-access language exists in Section 4.4 or elsewhere per the finding's scan.

elements.element: Vendor may audit no more than once per year.
elements.evidence: Retained language: "Such inspections may be made no more than once each calendar year".

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 15 days' notice of an audit.
elements.evidence: Edit replaces "reasonable notice" with "at least fifteen (15) days' notice" — a fixed minimum period satisfying the fallback.

elements.element: Vendor bears audit costs unless underpayment exceeds 10 percent.
elements.evidence: "Commerce One shall bear all costs and expenses of such inspection" retained, and the reimbursement trigger is now "an underpayment of more than ten percent (10%) for the period under audit".

verification.notes: Fallback level is complete: annual frequency already existed, notice is now a fixed fifteen (15) days, and Commerce One bears inspection costs unless underpayment exceeds ten percent (10%). Preferred level is not reached: no 30-day written notice, no business-hours limit, no auditor confidentiality undertaking, no off-site-where-possible preference, and the frequency cap is per calendar year rather than per rolling 12-month period. These are correctly noted rather than pursued, consistent with treating fallback-level terms as acceptable. Both edits are necessary to the chosen fallback checklist: the 5%-to-10% threshold change is required because a 5% trigger shifts cost to Corio in cases the fallback element requires Commerce One to bear, and "reasonable notice" is an undefined trigger rather than a fixed minimum. No survival tails, procedures, expense language or extraneous requirements were added, and the drafter changed no words outside the two target elements. Intent preserved: three-year retention, independent CPA acceptable to Corio, the shortfall/overpayment true-up mechanic and the general cost allocation all survive intact; no dangling cross-references or contradictory retained sentences result, and the 10% reimbursement trigger is internally consistent with the retained "Commerce One shall bear all costs" sentence. No system-access right exists to delete, so the walk-away risk (unlimited, unannounced or remote-access audits) is not present.

mappings.element: Professional errors and omissions coverage is at least USD 1,000,000.
Cyber and privacy coverage is at least USD 2,000,000.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] The Agreement contains no insurance obligation even though Commerce One's personnel work in our hosted environment and its MarketSite.net Service handles transaction data, so we add our fallback insurance position: errors and omissions cover of at least USD 1,000,000 and cyber/privacy cover of at least USD 2,000,000.

ops.text: Insurance. Commerce One shall maintain professional liability (errors and omissions) insurance of not less than USD 1,000,000 and cyber and privacy liability insurance of not less than USD 2,000,000.

proposal.summary: Insert a short insurance clause in Miscellaneous requiring Commerce One E&O of USD 1,000,000 and cyber/privacy cover of USD 2,000,000.

quote: 14.9 Bankruptcy. The parties hereto agree that Corio, as a licensee of Commerce One's intellectual property, shall be afforded all of the protections afforded to a licensee under Section 365(n) of the United States Bankruptcy Code
rationale: No insurance obligation exists anywhere in the Agreement: the Miscellaneous section (14.1-14.10) runs from assignment to complete understanding with no coverage provision, the indemnification and limitation of liability sections are silent, and the only occurrence of \"insurance\" in the document is a deduction item in the net revenue definition (p0012). Commerce One supplies operations, consulting and engineering personnel who work in our hosted environment (Sections 13.1-13.3) and operates the MarketSite.net Service, so it is a services/hosting vendor that touches our and our Customers' data with no coverage backing its indemnities. We therefore insert a short clause at the fallback level (E&O USD 1,000,000; cyber/privacy USD 2,000,000) rather than the fuller preferred package, as the shortest change that satisfies the position.

elements.element: Commercial general liability coverage is at least USD 1,000,000 per occurrence.
elements.evidence: The inserted Insurance paragraph covers only professional liability (E&O) and cyber/privacy liability; there is no commercial general liability limit anywhere in the rendered text. To reach preferred, add "commercial general liability insurance of not less than USD 1,000,000 per occurrence".

elements.element: Commercial general liability coverage is at least USD 2,000,000 in the aggregate.
elements.evidence: No aggregate CGL limit appears; the insertion stops at E&O and cyber figures. Add "and USD 2,000,000 in the aggregate" to a CGL obligation.

elements.element: Professional errors and omissions coverage is at least USD 2,000,000.
elements.evidence: Inserted language reads "professional liability (errors and omissions) insurance of not less than USD 1,000,000" — below the preferred USD 2,000,000 threshold.

elements.evidence: Commerce One hosts/processes transaction data, so the condition applies, but the inserted cyber and privacy limit is USD 2,000,000, short of USD 5,000,000.

elements.element: Vendor maintains workers' compensation coverage as required by law.
elements.evidence: No workers' compensation obligation is inserted, despite Commerce One personnel working in Corio's environment.

elements.element: Vendor provides certificates of insurance on request.
elements.evidence: The insertion contains no certificate-of-insurance delivery mechanic.

elements.element: Professional errors and omissions coverage is at least USD 1,000,000.
elements.evidence: Inserted operative text: "Commerce One shall maintain professional liability (errors and omissions) insurance of not less than USD 1,000,000" — Commerce One is the Vendor/counterparty, and the floor equals the fallback threshold.

elements.element: Cyber and privacy coverage is at least USD 2,000,000.
elements.evidence: Inserted operative text: "and cyber and privacy liability insurance of not less than USD 2,000,000" — matches the fallback amount and the named coverage type.

verification.notes: Finding status "missing" is corroborated: the rendered Miscellaneous provisions (14.9 bankruptcy, 14.10 complete understanding) contain no insurance covenant, and the only other document reference to "insurance" is a deduction item in a net revenue definition, so an insertion rather than an amendment is the right operation. The fallback checklist is complete on the operative text: an unconditional "shall maintain" obligation on Commerce One (the vendor) with an E&O floor of USD 1,000,000 and a cyber and privacy floor of USD 2,000,000, both stated as "not less than" minimums. The level is therefore position-complete at fallback. Preferred is not complete: CGL per-occurrence and aggregate limits, workers' compensation, and certificates on request are wholly absent, and the E&O (1M vs 2M) and cyber (2M vs 5M) amounts sit below preferred thresholds. Each is a discrete drafting gap, not a wording nuance. Minimality holds. The insertion is a single sentence limited to the two selected fallback elements; the drafter correctly omitted model-language extras such as "at its own expense", the term-plus-one-year survival tail, the CGL limits and the certificate mechanic, any of which would have added requirements outside the chosen checklist. No existing wording was deleted or paraphrased. Intent is preserved. Sections 14.9 and 14.10 survive verbatim; the new covenant creates no undefined term, dangling cross-reference, or contradiction with the entire-agreement clause (which governs prior agreements, not provisions within this Agreement). Drafting note only, not a failure: the paragraph is unnumbered and sits after the "IN WITNESS WHEREOF" sentence — give it a section number (e.g., 14.11) and place it before the execution line so it reads unambiguously as an operative Miscellaneous term. No double-counting concern: no other rule in this review addresses coverage limits, and the clause benefits Customer.
